title: Why Paraprofessionals Leave Mid-Year and How to Keep Classrooms Covered
metaTitle: Paraprofessional Turnover: Why Aides Leave, What Works
description: Why aides leave mid-year, sourced turnover figures, what an open IEP aide seat costs, and the onboarding and contracted aides that keep seats filled.
answer: Paraprofessionals leave mid-year mostly over pay, part-time hours that can fall short of benefits, behavior demands they were not trained for, and no path forward. Colorado's paraprofessional turnover was 27% between the 2024-25 and 2025-26 school years, against 16% for teachers. Districts keep classrooms covered by training aides before day one and adding contracted 1:1 aides for high-need rooms.
keyTakeaways: Colorado's paraprofessional turnover was 27.4% from 2024-25 to 2025-26, against 15.7% for teachers, and 33.7% in Denver County 1.
In Washington, paraeducator exits hit 23% after 2021-22, over double the 8% after 2008-09, and over 40% did not return to their para position.
The median teacher assistant earned $36,780 in May 2025, against $50,980 for all workers, by BLS figures.
A 1:1 aide written into an IEP is part of the services the IEP must state under 34 CFR 300.320(a)(4), and 34 CFR 300.323(c)(2) requires services to be made available in accordance with the IEP.
Contracted 1:1 aides arrive cleared and screened, cover absences from a pool, and can be hired permanently with no conversion fee.
bodyHtml:
How big is paraprofessional turnover and vacancy?

Large, and larger than teacher turnover wherever a state publishes both. In Colorado, 7,116 of the 26,009 paraprofessionals counted in 2024-25 were gone by the 2025-26 count, a turnover rate of 27.4%. Teacher turnover in the same file was 15.7% (source: Colorado Department of Education, Personnel Turnover Rates, 2025-26 compared with 2024-25).

The national vacancy picture points the same way. As of October 2024, classroom aides had an average vacancy rate of 7%, and 32% of public schools said they felt understaffed in classroom aides (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, December 12, 2024 release). Before the 2024-25 school year began, schools had filled 74% of their classroom aide vacancies (source: NCES School Pulse Panel, October 17, 2024 release). The national market is big and keeps churning: teacher assistants held about 1.5 million jobs in 2025, with about 176,200 openings projected each year (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, teacher assistants).

Washington's longer record shows how fast this changed. From the late 1990s through the early 2010s, paraeducator exits ran 8% to 11% a year. After 2021-22 the rate hit 23%, and counting every kind of move, over 40% of paraeducators did not return to their paraprofessional position for 2022-23 (source: CALDER, American Institutes for Research, Working Paper 283-0423, April 2023). The authors call it "a crisis in paraeducator retention." A 2026 Stanford report cites state-level data showing annual paraeducator attrition as high as 28% to 40% (source: Stanford University, Getting Down to Facts, Paraeducators in California, May 2026).

So the claim you may have heard, that turnover tops 30% in many districts, holds where a state publishes it by district. In Colorado, 86 of the 197 districts that report paraprofessionals were above 30% from 2024-25 to 2025-26, including 17 of the 56 with 50 or more aides. Denver's figure is 33.7%. Pull your own number the same way: people who left divided by last year's headcount. For the wider picture, see the paraprofessional shortage nobody's talking about.

Why do paraprofessionals leave mid-year?

They leave for 5 reasons the research names again and again: pay, hours that fall short of benefits, physical and behavior demands, thin training, and no next step. Mid-year is when those add up: the first hard months with a student, a better offer, or a schedule that never reached full time.

Pay against other work

The median annual wage for teacher assistants was $36,780 in May 2025, against $50,980 for all workers. The lowest 10% earned less than $27,150 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, teacher assistants). In Washington, the average paraeducator earned just under $30,000 in 2021-22, before any adjustment for part-time hours (source: CALDER, American Institutes for Research, Working Paper 283-0423, April 2023). Administrators in a 2026 California study said turnover is driven by "the high cost of living and the daily stress of managing challenging student behaviors" (source: Stanford University, Getting Down to Facts, Paraeducators in California, May 2026). Compare your own para scale with local wages in your county, because that is the offer your aides are weighing.

Hours and benefits eligibility

Part-time work is common for teacher assistants, and many do not work during the summer (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, teacher assistants). In a review of 10 large districts' contracts, an average of 21.85 hours a week was needed for health coverage. Because most paraeducators work part-time, the authors conclude they are likely to have less coverage than teachers (source: Annenberg Institute at Brown University, EdWorkingPaper 21-490, 2021).

Injury and behavior demands

BLS notes that teacher assistants "sometimes get injured on the job" and may need to lift students (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, teacher assistants). In a 2025-26 survey of 146 paraeducators in a California district, the lowest self-ratings were for managing student behavior, de-escalating challenging behaviors, and feeling respected or valued as part of the team (source: Stanford University, Getting Down to Facts, Paraeducators in California, May 2026).

Training that never arrives

The same Stanford report found that because paraeducators are hourly, training outside contracted hours is optional. One principal said, "If it is optional, many don't join." Administrators described onboarding as "random" and unwelcoming, which can make new hires "feel like outsiders from day one" (source: Stanford University, Getting Down to Facts, Paraeducators in California, May 2026). Only 1 of 10 large districts studied by Brown and University of Washington researchers mentioned a formal mentoring program for paraeducators, against 8 of 10 for teachers (source: Annenberg Institute at Brown University, EdWorkingPaper 21-490, 2021).

No path forward

Only 1 of those 10 districts mentioned leadership roles for paraeducators, while all 10 did for teachers. Six in 10 offered support to become a certified teacher, which is a path out of the role (source: Annenberg Institute at Brown University, EdWorkingPaper 21-490, 2021). In Washington, fewer than 3% of paraeducators moved into teaching in any year (source: CALDER, American Institutes for Research, Working Paper 283-0423, April 2023). Yet 30.1% of the California paraeducators surveyed wanted to pursue a teaching or special education credential (source: Stanford University, Getting Down to Facts, Paraeducators in California, May 2026).

What does an open aide seat cost when the IEP names the support?

It costs a service you owe, every day it is missing. When an IEP lists a 1:1 aide, that aide is a supplementary aid and service, and federal rules require the district to provide it as written.

Every IEP must include "a statement of the special education and related services and supplementary aids and services" to be provided to the child (source: 34 CFR 300.320(a)(4), eCFR). Supplementary aids and services are the "aids, services, and other supports" that let a child learn alongside nondisabled peers (source: 34 CFR 300.42, eCFR). Once the IEP is written, services must be "made available to the child in accordance with the child's IEP" (source: 34 CFR 300.323(c)(2), eCFR). When a state complaint finds services were not provided, the remedy can include "compensatory services or monetary reimbursement" (source: 34 CFR 300.151(b)(1), eCFR).

State complaint decisions show what this looks like. In a 2024-25 Wisconsin case, an IEP called for "1:1 special education support throughout the entire day" for 7 hours every day. At lunch the student was supervised by staff who were also watching other students, and the state found the district "did not consistently implement the student's IEP regarding one-to-one support." It ordered the IEP team to reconvene within 30 days (source: Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction, IDEA Complaint Decision 24-124). Missed minutes add up the same way for every role; our guide to IEP backlogs and compensatory services shows how to track them, and what an unfilled classroom costs puts dollar figures on a vacancy.

The person in the seat has to qualify, too. IDEA lets states use paraprofessionals "who are appropriately trained and supervised, in accordance with State law, regulation, or written policy" to assist in providing special education (source: 34 CFR 300.156(b)(2)(iii), eCFR). In Title I programs, ESSA requires states to ensure paraprofessionals "meet applicable State certification and licensure requirements" and to keep professional standards for them, "including qualifications that were in place on the day before December 10, 2015" (source: 20 U.S.C. 6311(g)(2)(J) and (M), govinfo). Pennsylvania, for example, requires Title I instructional paraprofessionals to hold a diploma plus an associate degree, 48 college credits, or a passing score on a state or local assessment, and special education paraprofessionals to meet one of the same degree, credit or assessment options and complete at least 20 hours of staff development each school year. Personal care assistants who give a student 1:1 support owe the same 20 hours (source: Pennsylvania Department of Education, CSPG 101). State rules are laid out on our Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware paraprofessional pages.

Should you add contracted 1:1 aides to your district paraprofessionals?

Yes, for the seats where a gap is a compliance problem. Your district paraprofessionals are the base of the program and should stay that way. Contracted 1:1 aides and behavior-trained paraprofessionals add speed and a backup for the highest-need classrooms.

The combined model wins because the IEP clock does not wait for a hiring cycle. Needs do change mid-year. In a 2024-25 Wisconsin case, an IEP team met on October 4 and decided a student needed a 1:1 aide for the entire school day; the full-day aide started October 18 (source: Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction, IDEA Complaint Decision 25-100). A partner with cleared candidates on hand shortens that gap.

How do you retain special education aides in the first 30 days?

Four changes do the most: give the aide the IEP before day one, pay for training inside the workday, pair the aide with the supervising teacher, and check in on a fixed schedule. The first is a federal rule. The next 2 come from research. The last is practice.

  1. Hand over the IEP and the job before day one. Each IEP must be accessible to "any other service provider who is responsible for its implementation," and each must be told their "specific responsibilities" and the supports the child must receive (source: 34 CFR 300.323(d), eCFR). For a 1:1 aide, that means the goals, the behavior plan and the data sheet on the first morning, not the third week.
  2. Put training inside paid hours. Administrators in the Stanford study recommended "a minimum number of paid annual training hours" in every paraeducator contract, because optional training goes unattended (source: Stanford University, Getting Down to Facts, Paraeducators in California, May 2026). Start with de-escalation and safety, delivered by your district's own trainers, since that is where new aides rate themselves lowest.
  3. Train the aide and the supervising teacher together. The same study tied high turnover to placing paraeducators with teachers not equipped to support them, and found paras "often get trained but can't apply or reflect" without joint training (source: Stanford University, Getting Down to Facts, Paraeducators in California, May 2026). Name one teacher as the aide's go-to person for the first month.
  4. Check in at the end of week 1, week 2 and week 4. This is practice, not a research finding. Ask 3 questions: what is hard with the student, what do you need from the teacher, and do you plan to stay. Invite aides to staff meetings; administrators said exclusion makes paras feel "segregated" from certificated staff (source: Stanford University, Getting Down to Facts, Paraeducators in California, May 2026).

None of this needs a new budget line. It needs a calendar. Our First 30 Days: Paraprofessional Onboarding Checklist below puts every step in order.

How do contracted aides stabilize a high-need classroom mid-year?

They put a cleared, screened adult back in the seat while your district hire is still in process, and they keep the seat covered when that adult is out. That restores the IEP service right away instead of after a hiring cycle.

Start with the classrooms where a gap hurts most: 1:1 assignments written into IEPs, self-contained rooms that depend on the ratio, and students with behavior intervention plans. Write a coverage plan into the IEP before you need it. A Wisconsin IEP team did exactly that after an aide stepped away for about 27 minutes, specifying that "a familiar adult would fill in" when the student's 1:1 aide was absent (source: Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction, IDEA Complaint Decision 23-104). A contracted aide who works the same room every day becomes that familiar adult.

Then use the placement as a tryout. Temp-to-perm lets your principals and case managers watch an aide with the student before offering a district job, which turns a stopgap into your own hire. For behavior-heavy rooms, pair contracted aides with school-based behavioral health staffing, and fill the teacher seats through special education staffing.

faqs.q: What is the paraprofessional turnover rate?
faqs.a: It depends on the state, and few states publish it. Colorado's Department of Education reports paraprofessional turnover of 27.4% from 2024-25 to 2025-26, with 7,116 of 26,009 paraprofessionals leaving, against 15.7% for teachers. In Washington, CALDER researchers found 23% of paraeducators left the state's public school workforce after 2021-22, and over 40% did not return to the same para position.

faqs.q: Why is there a paraprofessional shortage?
faqs.a: Pay, hours and working conditions. The median teacher assistant earned $36,780 in May 2025, against $50,980 for all workers, according to BLS. Part-time schedules can fall below the hours needed for health coverage, and training is often optional for hourly staff. As of October 2024, 32% of public schools said they felt understaffed in classroom aides, according to NCES.

faqs.q: How do you retain special education aides?
faqs.a: Give each aide the IEP and their specific duties before day one, as 34 CFR 300.323(d) requires. Pay for training inside the workday, starting with de-escalation and safety. Pair the aide with one supervising teacher and train them together. Check in at the end of weeks 1, 2 and 4, and include aides in staff meetings so they are part of the team.

faqs.q: Does a district have to provide a 1:1 aide written into an IEP?
faqs.a: Yes. A 1:1 aide listed in an IEP is a supplementary aid and service under 34 CFR 300.320(a)(4), and 34 CFR 300.323(c)(2) requires services to be made available in accordance with the IEP. If a state complaint finds services were missed, 34 CFR 300.151(b)(1) names compensatory services or monetary reimbursement as remedies.

faqs.q: What qualifications does a Title I paraprofessional need?
faqs.a: ESSA requires states to keep professional standards for Title I paraprofessionals, including the qualifications in place before December 10, 2015, under 20 U.S.C. 6311(g)(2)(M). In Pennsylvania, that means a high school diploma plus an associate degree, 48 college credits, or a passing score on a state or local assessment. Pennsylvania special education paraprofessionals need the same degree, credit or assessment option and at least 20 hours of staff development each school year.

faqs.q: When should a district use contracted 1:1 aides?
faqs.a: Use them for seats where a gap becomes a missed IEP service: 1:1 assignments, self-contained classrooms that depend on the ratio, and students with behavior plans.
